Lot Note:
Ernest Martin Hennings’s Land of Sage and Cedar manifests the artist’s “plein air” manner—his Impressionistic brushwork, rich palette, stylized lines and contours, and decorative patterns. Echoing a visually smooth texture, the painting displays the soft and peaceful beauty of the open Taos topography. The stretching and verdant hills, dappled in warm, enchanting light, are a subject of remarkable natural charm.

Within the landscape, we notice three Indian figures on horseback quietly passing through the brush. The scene is full of serenity and activates all the senses. The title, Land of Sage and Cedar, immediately conjures up distinct aromas, colors, and forms. As a result, the painting’s viewer, the sole witness to the procession, is also summoned to the experience.

The foliage, a lush backdrop to the trio making their way through the wide expanse, is not an attribute merely serving the composition. Instead, it emphasizes the harmony the Indian and the landscape achieved and maintained in the Taos region for centuries, as the colors reverberating on the canvas, such as the green hue on the horses, indicate.

Lot Note:
William Keith was one of the foremost early California landscapists, regarded as the "Dean of California Painters" for his prolific and influential body of work. His early efforts, from the 1860s through the early 1880s, often featured grand, panoramic, and meticulously detailed views of the region's scenery and Native inhabitants, reflecting the prevailing Romantic tradition of artists like Albert Bierstadt. Influenced by his close friend, naturalist John Muir, Keith initially sought topographical accuracy, but after 1882, his paintings adopted a poetic and "intimate" style, focusing on soft light, mood, and atmosphere. The present work, dating to 1870, was executed at the height of his early and expansive style, and is emblematic of the sort of Western (and Pacific Northwestern) views that established his reputation.

Lot Note:
The Illusion of Red, Yellow and Blue in Space No. 2 is a densely composed dot painting, a thrilling example of the final period in Vance Kirkland’s artistic career. Amorphous sinuous forms emerge from a seemingly scattered but carefully crafted web of dots applied to the canvas with wooden dowels. As the larger shapes bloom and swirl, the dots add texture and dimension to the work, popping out of the painted surface. In a coherent and organic arrangement of warm and brilliant colors, the painting exudes chromatic vibrancy and vivacious design. Often described as a visionary, Kirkland came to embrace the cosmos as a tantalizing aesthetic subject and sought to convey its infinite and perennial qualities through innovative imagery.

Lot Note:
Jaune Quick-to-See Smith's Cheyenne Series (see also Lot 107) is a foundational body of work where the artist first developed her signature visual language: a juxtaposition of Indigenous symbolism and modernist abstraction. By layering images of horses, tepees, cacti, and petroglyphs—drawn from her Salish, Kootenai and Shoshone heritage—onto canvases marked with the expressive brushwork and gestural energy of artists like Robert Rauschenberg or Paul Klee, Quick-to-See Smith established a vital dialogue. The series, named after her own horse, interrogated traditional culture and memory as a means of commenting on contemporary Indigenous identity and the Western landscape, effectively laying the groundwork for the more explicitly political themes seen in her seminal later works.

Lot Note:
Norval Morrisseau is widely considered a pioneer of contemporary Indigenous art in Canada. His early works, often executed on found or discarded materials such as birch bark, emulated ancient pictographs. As he became acquainted with the techniques of European modern art, starting in the 1950s, Morrisseau’s style progressively incorporated a bright palette of deeply saturated colors and modernist draftsmanship with stylized, heavily contoured forms. Shaman Thunderbird Apprentice is an exceptional example of Morrisseau’s late, mature output.

Throughout his career, Morrisseau’s pictorial vocabulary remained his own, a savvy and controlled combination of legends, dream-like imagery and bold, graphic lines and motifs reminiscent of Fauvism and even contemporaneous Pop Art. Here, the figure of the shaman as spiritual mediator holds profound significance for the artist at a personal level. As a young man, Morrisseau was given the name Copper Thunderbird by a Medicine Woman in the hopes that it would heal the grave illness afflicting him. He has ever since credited the name for saving his life, and signed his work accordingly, in Cree syllabic. At its core, Morrisseau’s work remains deeply rooted in personal experience and cultural heritage, invoking rituals and legends that have fashioned and carried his people from time immemorial.
